context:
Models have become strong at producing code and back-end logic, but professional creative work is judged by a different standard. A deliverable can contain every element the client asked for and still be unusable: the layout is broken, the branding is off, characters change appearance between images, text is cramped or misspelled, and the whole thing simply looks less polished than what a professional would hand over. In this project we build a proxy of Scale AI's RLI evalset focused on media generation and editing, where every deliverable is a visual, audio, video, 3D or interactive artifact and where how it looks weighs more than whether it's there: 65% of every rubric grades aesthetics, against 30% correctness and 5% format.

Contributors create tasks consisting of a realistic client brief with input files, an expert-produced golden output that scores 97% or higher on the rubric, a rubric of 40+ binary pass/fail criteria, and a preference ranking comparing the golden output against the model's attempt. Tasks are calibrated so the reference model (Gemini 3.7 Flash with maximum thinking and generation tools) scores uniformly between 25% and 50%. Tasks are drawn from 11 creative domains.
grading: Grade to the lowest dimension across all rubrics (if one dimension is a 2, the task is a 2).
If the task meets any criteria under 1-2 Fail, the task is a fail.
If the task does not fail and meets a 3-4 [Non-Fail] on any dimension, the whole task is a 3-4 [Non-Fail].
All dimensions must be a 5 for the task to receive a 5.
Between 1 and 2: pick 1 if the attempter put little to no effort. Between 3 and 4: judge how seriously the minor issue affects quality.
Prompt or task instructions always take precedence over other dimensions.

dimensions.name: Ranking Disagreement
dimensions.notes: Covers QC agreement with the contributor's preference ratings (three comparisons × five dimensions on the 1–7 scale).

options.label: Fail - Major Ranking Disagreement
options.text: You and CB have a severe disagreement, such as one marks AD1/AD2 as at most 2 in at least 2 dimensions and the auditor thinks it's at least a 6, or vice versa.

options.label: Non-Fail - Loose Ranking Disagreement
options.text: For 2 dimensions, you and the contributor disagree on non-adjacent buckets; or for 3+ dimensions, you and the contributor disagree on adjacent buckets.

options.label: No Issues
options.text: You agree with all of the contributor's ratings; OR any variance is a matter of subjective taste that the justification adequately supports.

dimensions.name: Analysis
dimensions.notes: The SxS justification must provide a detailed explanation of what the brief asks for and compare the deliverables accordingly.

options.label: Fail - Generic Justification
options.text: The justification does not provide any explanation other than stating the ranking, e.g. "A is better."

options.label: Non-Fail - Generic Justification
options.text: The justification provides some explanation or evidence supporting the SxS ranking, but it did not address all the issues.

options.label: No Issues
options.text: The justification is very detailed: it explains what the brief asks for comprehensively and compares the deliverables in detail.

dimensions.name: Criteria Count (40–100)
dimensions.notes: The rubric is the checklist of binary (pass/fail) criteria used to score the golden output and every model attempt. Count every criterion, including negative-weight (penalty) criteria.

options.label: Fail - Criteria Count
options.text: The rubric has fewer than 40 criteria.

options.label: Non-Fail - Criteria Count
options.text: The rubric has more than 100 criteria.

options.label: No Issues
options.text: The rubric contains 40 to 100 criteria.

dimensions.name: Weights
dimensions.notes:
Weight is signed importance from −10 to +10 (positive = something the deliverable should have; negative = a defect it should not have).

Taxonomy: Critically Important (8 to 10) — the deliverable is unacceptable without it; Important (4 to 7) — expected in professional work, missing it clearly hurts the result; Slightly Important (1 to 3) — adds polish or value beyond the core ask; Slightly Detrimental (−1 to −3) — a minor flaw a client would notice; Detrimental (−4 to −7) — a serious defect, such as unprofessional practice; Critically Detrimental (−8 to −10) — a dealbreaker, such as violating an explicit constraint or a non-working deliverable.

Important elements must be weighted high. Aesthetics must account for at least 65% of the summed positive weight (hard requirement). The client's mix: 5% formatting, 30% brief compliance, 65% aesthetics + functionality + usability/professionalism.

options.label: Fail - Criteria Weights
options.text: Aesthetics accounts for less than 65% of the summed positive weight; OR 5+ or 10% of the rubric (whichever is greater) criteria that AD1 and/or AD2 fail AND are weighted as Critically Important/Detrimental when they should be Slightly Important/Detrimental, or vice versa.

options.label: Non-Fail - Criteria Weights
options.text: At most 5 criteria that AD1 and/or AD2 fail AND are weighted as Critically Important/Detrimental when they should be Slightly Important/Detrimental, or vice versa.

options.label: No Issues
options.text: There are no criteria that AD1 and/or AD2 fail AND are weighted as Critically Important/Detrimental when they should be Slightly Important/Detrimental, or vice versa.

dimensions.name: Golden-Solution Neutrality
dimensions.notes:
Rubrics must not enforce subjective choices without leaving room for other plausible solutions. Professional expectations/standards are OK as rubrics. If a choice is subjective, it should be comparable to the golden or phrased leniently.

A major error example: "The cupboards are red" where nothing in the brief/input files asks for red and it cannot be justified by professional expectations.

options.label: Fail - Golden-Solution Neutrality
options.text: 20% or more of the criteria enforce subjective choices without room for equally plausible alternatives, and are neither comparable to the golden reference nor phrased leniently.

options.label: Non-Fail - Golden-Solution Neutrality
options.text: 11%–19% of the criteria have such errors.

options.label: No Issues
options.text: 10% or less of the criteria enforce an arbitrary subjective choice.

dimensions.name: Overlap / Redundancy
dimensions.notes: Redundancy = two criteria independently assess the same elements (e.g., Criteria 1: response does a, b, c / Criteria 2: response does a, b). A single criterion that introduces and then specifies related requirements is acceptable.

options.label: Fail - Overlap / Redundancy
options.text: 2 or more criteria are redundant or overlapping (independently assessing the same elements).

options.label: Non-Fail - Overlap / Redundancy
options.text: Exactly 1 criterion is redundant or overlapping with another.

options.label: No Issues
options.text: No redundant criteria are present.

dimensions.name: Coverage
dimensions.notes: The rubric list should be as comprehensive as possible. Count three things when measuring what is missing: (1) the brief's explicit requests, (2) widely-accepted implicit professional expectations even if not specified, and (3) NUANCES OF THE FIELD — things only a professional would check and AI/students would miss (e.g., a wallpaper pattern must continue seamlessly when tiled; this deserves a high-importance criterion even though no brief spells it out). The rubric should highlight the important elements, capturing explicit and implicit human/professional preferences and expectations.

options.label: Fail - Missing Coverage
options.text: Fail if any of these is present: (1) missing rubric criteria across the three categories are ≥10% of the rubric; (2) the rubric is highly skewed toward a handful of aspects and does not provide full coverage (the client's 5% formatting / 30% brief compliance / 65% aesthetics + functionality + usability/professionalism mix is fine); (3) the rubric is too high-level — only superficial checks, missing what professionals care about (high-level is OK as long as the details are also called out); (4) the rubric does not cover 3 or more of the brief's explicit requests.

options.label: Non-Fail - Missing Coverage
options.text: Missing criteria that correspond to the brief's explicit requirements are at least 1 but less than 10% of the rubric; OR 1+ implicit expectations are missing.

options.label: No Issues
options.text: The rubric covers all the explicit requests, the implicit professional expectations, and the expert-level nuances of the field.

dimensions.name: Relevance & Correctness
dimensions.notes:
Criteria must be mostly faithful to the brief and to general consensus or justifiable preferences of the domain. Region-based constraints refer to locale and localization when indicated in the brief and/or input files.

Criteria must match the brief exactly — correct spelling and naming of terms, and specific values rather than generalizations. If the brief specifies a particular color, size, count, or format, the criterion should name that exact value. Example: the brief specified amber #F4A300. Good: "The banner uses #F4A300". Bad: "The banner uses a warm color". Bad: "The banner uses #F4B255". We are not evaluating for general accuracy.

options.label: Fail - Criteria Accuracy
options.text: 2 or more criteria are irrelevant to the task (no clear justification that they are a requirement), arbitrarily introduced, or assume region-based constraints the brief does not indicate.

options.label: Non-Fail - Criteria Accuracy
options.text: Exactly 1 criterion is irrelevant, unjustified, or does not make sense given the brief.

options.label: No Issues
options.text: Every criterion makes sense given the brief: relevant, justified as a requirement, and free of undeclared region-based assumptions.

dimensions.name: Atomicity
dimensions.notes: Criteria should be MOSTLY atomic: they must not combine irrelevant/unrelated checks. Bundling IS acceptable when two things should be evaluated at the same time. E.g., checking if cupboards, floors and lighting follow a coherent style in one criterion is OK; checking if lighting is present and french doors are chosen is not.

options.label: Fail - Criteria Atomicity
options.text: 4+ or 10% of the rubric (whichever is bigger) criteria combine unrelated checks together.

options.label: Non-Fail - Criteria Atomicity
options.text: 1–3 or ≤9% of criteria bundle unrelated constraints, or a few bundles are borderline but defensible.

options.label: No Issues
options.text: Criteria are mostly atomic: no criterion bundles multiple unrelated constraints; combined criteria only pair elements that should be evaluated together.

dimensions.name: Self-contained or Vague Criteria
dimensions.notes: Every criterion should be evaluable on its own; assume the grader has the RD and the brief in context. A criterion that refers to the golden reference for comparison is accepted ("the tabletop is as thick as the golden reference"). Vague relative references — "scaled down", "shortened", "improved contrast" — fail: they point at a fact stored somewhere else instead of stating it, and two graders will fill the gap differently.

options.label: Fail - Self-Contained or Vague Criteria
options.text: 4+ or 10% of the rubric (whichever is bigger) criteria are vague or not self-contained.

options.label: Non-Fail - Self-Contained or Vague Criteria
options.text: 1–3 or ≤9% of criteria are vague or not self-contained, and neither fail condition applies.

options.label: No Issues
options.text: All criteria are evaluable on their own; self-contained within the RD, the inputs and the brief, and/or by professional nuance; none require external references and none are vague.

dimensions.name: Aesthetic & Comparative Depth
dimensions.notes: When design and functionality are important in the domain, include aesthetic and/or functionality criteria when relevant.

options.label: Fail - Aesthetic Criteria
options.text: Design is central to the brief but the rubric has almost no aesthetic and/or functionality criteria when relevant, or judges aesthetics as a single lump.

options.label: Non-Fail - Aesthetic Criteria
options.text: The rubric has aesthetic and/or functionality criteria, when relevant, but misses key elements.

options.label: No Issues
options.text: The rubric grades each relevant visual/auditory element on its own, with depth proportional to how central design is.

dimensions.name: Criteria Justifications
dimensions.notes: Do not penalize when the identified inaccuracy is subjective, or the CB's POV is reasonable. The percentage is out of the total number of justifications, not criteria: 30 criteria × 3 responses = 90 justifications, so 10% is 9.

options.label: Fail - Criteria Justifications
options.text: 20% or more of the criteria justifications are objectively inaccurate.

options.label: Non-Fail - Criteria Justifications
options.text: 11%–19% of the criteria justifications are objectively inaccurate.

options.label: No Issues
options.text: All justifications are correct and aligned with their ratings, OR 10% or less are objectively inaccurate.

dimensions.name: Justification–Final Score Alignment
dimensions.notes: Preference ranking and rubric grading must not be in high contrast. Tolerance: when rubric totals are within a couple of percent (63% vs 62%), either preference direction is acceptable. A failure is a large, opposing gap — e.g. the justification says RD is significantly better than the ADs, yet an AD earns ~90% of the rubric score; or rubric scores show A slightly better than B but the preference rankings differ by 3+ points across 3 dimensions indicating B is better.

options.label: Fail - Justification - Final Score Alignment
options.text: The preference ranking and rubric scores are in high contrast: the rubric totals show a large gap that opposes the stated preference direction, well beyond a couple of percent.

options.label: Non-Fail - Justification Alignment
options.text: A modest mismatch between the preference direction and the rubric totals — a couple of percent, not a reversed story.

options.label: No Issues
options.text: The preference ranking and rubric totals tell the same story.

dimensions.name: Golden Artifact Sanity (RD ≥97%)
dimensions.notes: Check the "Final Rubric Scores" percentage for RD. It should be 97% or more as printed in the task. DO NOT adjust or deduct points from the RD final score — the original rubric score is the source of truth.

options.label: Fail - Golden Output Scoring
options.text: The golden output scores less than 97% on the rubric.

options.label: No Issues
options.text: Golden output scores 97% or higher on the rubric.

dimensions.name: Brief & Input Sufficiency
dimensions.notes: Task-level gate: the brief and input files must be sufficient to realistically carry out the task. If severely missing, the task fails regardless of the contributor's work — they should have flagged it at the brief-sufficiency gate. Fail example: an interior architecture task whose inputs don't include the plan, whose brief doesn't explain the space, and whose rubric assumes a specific plan.

options.label: Fail - Brief & Input Sufficiency
options.text: The brief and input files are severely missing for the task, and the contributor proceeded anyway instead of flagging it.

options.label: No Issues
options.text: The brief and input files are sufficient to realistically carry out the task.

dimensions.name: Unlisted Minor Errors
dimensions.notes: Describe the error in detail in the audit feedback.

options.label: Non-Fail - Unlisted Minor Errors
options.text: There are errors in the task not explicitly covered by the grading rubric that prevent it from being perfect.

options.label: No Issues
options.text: There are no unlisted errors that degrade the quality of the task.

dimensions.name: Accuracy (RD/AD1/AD2)
dimensions.notes: Verdict accuracy for RD, AD1 and AD2.

options.label: Fail - Criteria Verdict Accuracy
options.text: 10% or more of Pass/Fail verdicts per response are incorrect.

options.label: Non-Fail - Criteria Verdict Accuracy
options.text: Less than 10% but at least 1 of the Pass/Fail verdicts per response are incorrect.

options.label: No Issues
options.text: Every Pass/Fail verdict for RD, AD1 and AD2 is correct.

dimensions.name: Final percentage for AD1 and AD2
dimensions.notes: The QC auditor manually validates each pass/fail for each criterion; if QC's score for the models is above the threshold, the task fails.

options.label: Fail - Stumping Score
options.text: AD1 is > 70% or AD2 is > 50% on the final rubric summary.

options.label: No Issues
options.text: AD1 is 70% or less AND AD2 is 50% or less.

dimensions.name: Accuracy
dimensions.notes: Do not fail if the file is called by name in the brief without mentioning an exact path.

options.label: Fail - Incorrect/Inconsistent Paths
options.text: An explicit path is specified in the brief but the artifact is not found there, OR the brief's placements and the rubric's expectations are inconsistent (e.g. brief asks for 'final_version.pdf', rubric checks 'final version.pdf').

options.label: No Issues
options.text: Explicit paths in the brief resolve, and the brief and rubric agree on names and placements.

dimensions.name: Derived-Deliverable Provenance
dimensions.notes: Applies whenever the brief asks for an artifact that must be derived from a supplied or authored source file rather than created independently: renders or turntables from a 3D model, exports from a CAD file, stems bounced from a session, frames cut from a supplied video. Example: in tasks that ask for renders of 3D files (like Contemporary Residence), models that generate images from scratch instead of rendering them from the 3D files must be heavily punished.

options.label: Fail - Derived-Deliverable Provenance
options.text: The brief requires a derived deliverable AND the rubric has no criterion penalising generation-instead-of-derivation; OR such a criterion exists but is weighted outside Critically Detrimental (−8 to −10); OR a deliverable that was demonstrably generated rather than derived is passed on it.

options.label: No Issues
options.text: The rubric contains a Critically Detrimental criterion that explicitly penalises generating the deliverable instead of deriving it, names the evidence a grader should check, and the RD/AD1/AD2 verdicts on it are correct.
